strengths: Well-motivated and practical problem: personalizing VLAs for user-specific objects is important and clearly articulated
Training-free approach is a significant practical advantage—can adapt frozen models without retraining
Comprehensive evaluation with two simulation benchmarks and real-world robot experiments, including good ablations showing component contributions
Honest and detailed error analysis: Section D and Appendices categorize three classes of failures with qualitative examples, demonstrating transparency
Strong experimental documentation: extensive implementation details, hyperparameters, and dataset descriptions support reproducibility
Clear and well-presented method: core pipeline is intuitive and visually explained, with good use of figures and tables
weaknesses: Modest empirical improvements with significant remaining failure rates: VAP achieves 5-25% improvements in most settings but still shows 20-50% failure rates, limiting practical impact

Limited novelty—incremental contribution: grounding via reference images and visual prompting are standard techniques; the main contribution is combining existing components without algorithmic innovation
Cascading failures from upstream components: VAP depends critically on frozen DINO/SAM2 quality, but provides no robustness analysis of detector/segmenter failures
Unresolved multi-view inconsistency: Case 2 failures show template-based rewriting doesn't address contradictory masks across cameras (59.2% of multi-view failures); this fundamental issue remains

Token learning baseline comparisons inadequate: Appendix B shows token embeddings transfer well (~95% VQA accuracy), yet end-to-end gains are limited; VAP's advantage over token learning may be overstated

Severely limited scope of personalization: only handles object identification (not 'how to handle'), single object per episode, short-horizon tasks; cannot personalize interaction preferences (forces, approach direction, safety constraints)
Real-world evaluation is narrow: single robot platform, 8 object categories, single environment; generalization to different robots/settings unclear
Missing ablation and sensitivity analysis: no evaluation of grounding accuracy independently, template-based rewriting strategy not justified or ablated, mask opacity not analyzed

strengths: Well-motivated practical problem with clear real-world applicability (personalizing robotic manipulation)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across simulation benchmarks and real robot hardware with multiple baselines
Training-free approach that maintains modularity by not requiring parameter updates to frozen models
Honest and systematic error analysis categorizing three failure modes with concrete examples
Detailed experimental setup with clear descriptions of dataset construction and reproducible hardware configurations
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: VAP essentially combines existing detection (DINO), segmentation (SAM), masking, and template-based instruction rewriting—conceptually incremental for ICML standards
Modest empirical improvements with high relative-to-baseline ratios (5-18% absolute gains) and concerning absolute success rates in real-world settings (30-56%)
Fundamental architectural limitations remain unresolved: multi-view inconsistency causes 50-59% failures even with VAP, and manipulation difficulty persists at 40-49% failure rates
Misleading framing of 'personalizing' VLA models: VAP only personalizes inputs to frozen models through grounding/masking, not actual model adaptation
Narrow experimental scope limited to tabletop settings, 8 object categories, single personal object per scene, and simple short-horizon tasks with unclear generalization
Critical missing ablations: no ablation on detection/segmentation model choices, masking strategies, or instruction rewriting variations

Weak validation of core technical claims: token embedding preservation (Appendix B.2) relies only on cosine similarity metrics without behavioral equivalence proof, and token learning baseline achieves <95% accuracy suggesting brittleness
Real-world evaluation limited to single robot platform; no human studies evaluating user satisfaction or preference with personalization

strengths: Well-motivated practical problem: identifies genuine limitation of VLAs in distinguishing personal object instances, essential for real-world deployment
Elegant and simple solution: training-free approach that works with frozen models, immediately applicable to existing VLAs

Comprehensive evaluation: multiple simulation benchmarks (Personalized-SIMPLER, Personalized-VLABench) and real-world scenarios across different robot platforms with consistent improvements (20-40% gains)

Rigorous analysis with honest error case discussion: Appendix D categorizes failures into three types (single-view ambiguity, multi-view inconsistency, grounding-success-but-manipulation-failure) with concrete examples
Thorough investigation of design choices: token embedding space analysis, attention visualization, and comparison between token-learning and visual-prompting baselines
Strong methodological rigor: multiple runs, clear reporting of metrics (success rates, correct movement ratios), detailed experimental specifications enabling reproducibility
weaknesses: Significant failure rates in realistic scenarios: 59.2% failure in Personalized-VLABench multi-view, 50.9% in real-world, and 37.6% in single-view settings substantially limit practical applicability
Multi-view grounding inconsistency is a fundamental challenge: the paper identifies but doesn't solve the core issue that grounding locks onto different instances in different camera views
Limited scope and unclear scalability: restricted to single personal objects per scene, short-horizon tasks; no systematic exploration of multiple personal objects or highly similar instances

Insufficient analysis of reference image requirements: no systematic study of how many reference images are needed, sensitivity to diversity/quality, or behavior when reference appearances differ from deployment
Limited baseline comparisons: no comparison to alternative visual grounding methods or ablations on grounding components (DINO + SAM2); token-learning baseline underperformance not fully explained
Real-world evaluation is limited: only SO-101 robot, 4 tasks, 8 object categories; more extensive validation needed for generalizability claims
Incomplete problem formulation: doesn't address preference-based personalization (e.g., 'be gentle'), only instance-based; limited discussion of learning from failures
Technical clarity gaps: grounding function specification could be more rigorous, masking/instruction rewriting process lacks formal definition, code availability not mentioned

strengths: Well-motivated practical problem: Addresses a genuine gap in VLA applicability where models fail on personal objects due to distribution shift.

Comprehensive experimental validation: Two simulation benchmarks (Personalized-SIMPLER, Personalized-VLABench) with multiple robots, one real-world benchmark (SO-101), and multiple baselines showing substantial improvements (62.7% SR vs. 9.9% for generic VLA).

Thorough error analysis and ablations: Systematic categorization of three failure cases with root-cause analysis, ablations demonstrating necessity of each component, and honest discussion of limitations.
Strong token embedding transfer analysis: Demonstrates learned concept tokens transfer to VLA embeddings with minimal L2 distance (cosine similarity ≈ 0.9998), validating the transfer mechanism.
Multi-faceted evaluation: Rigorous experimental methodology including token embedding space analysis, sensitivity studies, visual prompt design ablations, and multi-user scenario demonstrations.
Honest limitations discussion: Authors acknowledge and analyze fundamental limitations (control gap, manipulation difficulty, multi-view inconsistency) rather than hiding them.
Good reproducibility: Hardware specifications, training configurations, evaluation protocols clearly documented with implementation details in appendices.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: Primarily combines two existing techniques (visual prompting from VLM literature and instruction rewriting from personalization work). The novelty is in application rather than methodological innovation.

Unresolved fundamental control gap: Visual prompting cannot reliably enforce instance-specific control when objects are visually similar (Figures 9-11). The paper acknowledges this core limitation but cannot overcome it, limiting practical applicability.

Multi-view inconsistency unresolved: Case 2 accounts for 59.2% of failures in Personalized-VLABench. Cross-view association remains problematic; proposed solutions (MAP-style fusion, cross-view association) are deferred to future work.

Not truly training-free or parameter-free: Requires K=5 reference images per object (Table 12), shifting adaptation cost from parameters to data. Performance saturates at K=5-7, indicating non-negligible collection overhead.

High failure rates remain: Real-world experiments show 31.9% failure rate; absolute success rates moderate (68.1% on SO-101). Token-learning baseline fails to outperform VAP, suggesting instance-level control is fundamentally hard.
Limited real-world scope: Only single SO-101 tabletop setup tested with 8 object categories. Unclear generalization beyond tabletop; no evaluation on different robots or environments.
Grounding robustness not evaluated: Method critically depends on accurate segmentation/grounding but lacks analysis of robustness to grounding errors or missing failure case attribution.

Manipulation difficulty unaddressed: When visual prompting succeeds but manipulation fails due to tight grasps or placement precision (Case 3), the method cannot help. This points to limits of vision-only personalization.

strengths: Addresses a practical and well-motivated problem: personalizing frozen VLAs for instance-level manipulation among similar objects
Training-free approach avoids expensive fine-tuning, making rapid personalization feasible
Comprehensive evaluation across multiple platforms (Google Robot, Widow X, real SO-101 setup) with both simulation and real-world experiments
Honest and detailed error analysis (Appendix D) identifying three failure mode categories, showing integrity in research
Extensive ablations and implementation details in appendices support reproducibility
Solid empirical results on simulation benchmarks, with VAP achieving 75% SR on Personalized-VLABench (vs. 31.9% for generic baseline)
weaknesses: Limited novelty: core technique is a straightforward combination of visual grounding (reference matching), mask-based prompting, and instruction rewriting—each component incremental, more systems/engineering contribution than scientific advance

Modest and inconsistent real-world improvements: success rates plateau at 50-75%; hard prompt baseline sometimes outperforms soft prompt (Table 2), indicating instability; token learning provides inconsistent gains often <5%

Fundamental limitations inadequately resolved: token learning fails to guarantee successful manipulation despite correct localization (Appendix B.3 admits localization is 'fragile over time'); cross-view inconsistency remains a major failure mode (59.2% failure in multi-view, Appendix D.2) with no tested solutions
Weak baseline comparisons: only compared against generic VLA and language-only prompts; missing ablations vs. simple alternatives (fine-tuning on reference episodes, basic language cues)

Brittle design choices: voting scheme for reference aggregation (Section 3.3) lacks principled justification; instruction rewriting via string templates doesn't scale; no sensitivity analysis for hyperparameters (mask opacity, detection thresholds)
Limited experimental rigor: no confidence intervals or statistical significance testing; real-world evaluation uses only 160 episodes across 8 tasks; tables confuse metrics and settings

Unclear generalization: evaluation restricted to tabletop picking tasks with 8 object categories; no analysis of scalability to diverse objects, manipulation complexities, or robot morphologies; multi-user evaluation relegated to brief appendix mention

Reproducibility gaps: no code release mentioned; reliance on specific vision models and prompt templates suggests results may not transfer; training data for detectors/segmentation not fully specified

Missing analyses: no ablation on mask vs. text-only prompts; inconsistent necessity of token learning (Table 2) suggests it may not be a core contribution; paper doesn't explain when hard prompts suffice (contradicting motivation that language abstracts instance details)
Overselling claims: abstract suggests VAP 'enables' personalized manipulation, but ~50% success on real-world tasks is insufficient for practical deployment in many scenarios
